narrative.text: First page of "SWOT Analysis: A Theoretical Review" by Emet Gürel (Ege University) and Merba Tat (Yaşar University), The Journal of International Social Research, volume 10, issue 51, August 2017. The abstract describes a qualitative, descriptive literature review of SWOT analysis as a situation-analysis technique used in marketing, public relations, advertising and other strategic planning, covering its place in strategic management, its components, an example for an international sportswear brand, its historical origins, and its advantages, disadvantages and limitations. The introduction defines strategic planning as part of strategic management and, following Barney and Hesterly, sets out the process: vision, mission, objectives, external and internal analysis (SWOT), strategic choice, implementation and finally competitive advantage.

Figure 1 (the strategic management process) and Sections 2 and 3. SWOT analysis is a tool for strategic planning and management; following the systems approach, an organisation exists in an internal and an external environment, and examining both is SWOT analysis (Figure 2). Thompson and colleagues are quoted calling it a simple but powerful tool. The acronym stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, and is also written TOWS, or in Turkish GZFT or FÜTZ. The internal dimension holds strengths and weaknesses, the external opportunities and threats, usually drawn as a four-quadrant 2×2 matrix. A footnote defines "acronym" from Merriam-Webster.

Table 1 (the components of SWOT analysis) and the explanation that follows. SWOT identifies an organisation's strengths and weaknesses from its internal elements and opportunities and threats from its environment, helping match resources and capabilities to the competitive environment. Strengths and opportunities are helpful to the organisation's objectives, weaknesses and threats harmful, and the manager's role is to fit internal strengths and weaknesses to external opportunities and threats. Table 2, a framework of variables to analyse, is credited to Wright and colleagues (1992); its content is not in the text layer.

Organisational strengths and weaknesses. A strength is a characteristic that gives an advantage over competitors; following Dinçer, an organisation can be rated strong, equal or weak on five criteria (relative market position, financial structure, production and technical capacity, R&D potential, and human capacity and management effectiveness). Definitions from Thompson and Strickland and from Pearce and Robinson are quoted, and strengths are said to be needed both to use opportunities and to answer threats. A weakness is a lack or poor performance relative to others that impairs effectiveness, with facilities, finance, management, marketing and brand image named as possible sources. Knowing weaknesses matters as much as knowing strengths, because no strategy can be built on weaknesses.

Table 3 (a strengths and weaknesses checklist, credited to Power and colleagues, 1986; its content is not in the text layer), then environmental opportunities and threats. An opportunity is a favourable time or condition the environment offers for reaching goals; Harrison and St. John define opportunities as external conditions that let an organisation use its strengths, overcome weaknesses or neutralise threats. A threat is an external condition that makes goals hard or impossible to reach and may stop the organisation surviving or keeping its competitive position, citing Ülgen and Mirze. Globalisation is said to bring both opportunities and threats, calling for more strategic attention.

Table 4 (an environmental variables checklist, also from Power and colleagues; content not in the text layer), then the scope of external and internal factors. Following David, external opportunities and threats are economic, social, cultural, demographic, environmental, political, legal, governmental, technological and competitive trends largely beyond the organisation's control, while internal strengths and weaknesses are controllable activities in management, marketing, finance, operations, R&D and information systems. Thompson and Strickland are quoted on drawing conclusions about matching strategy to capabilities and opportunities and on which weaknesses and threats are urgent. The block begins the Nike, Inc. example, describing the company as a multinational designing and selling footwear, apparel, equipment and services.

The rest of the Nike introduction and the caption of Table 5, the SWOT example for Nike, Inc. Nike is described as a leading maker of athletic shoes, apparel and sports equipment, founded in 1962 by Bill Bowerman and Philip H. Knight as Blue Ribbon Sports and named after the Greek goddess of victory. The text also has the sentence "Since Germany conquered the domestic market in America, Nike came with low-cost and high quality products", which seems to refer to German sportswear brands, and cites Nike's website. The table itself is not in the text layer.

Sources of the Nike table (two marketing-tutorial websites, 2016), the close of Section 3 and the start of Section 4 on SWOT's history. The authors stress that the value of SWOT lies in what story the four lists tell and what action they imply; its basic assumption is that internal activities must be aligned with external realities. SWOT appeared in the literature in the 1960s, but its origin is uncertain, credited by some to Harvard Business School and by others to Stanford. Albert Humphrey of the Stanford Research Institute described a 1960–1970 SRI project funded by Fortune 500 companies and led by Robert Stewart, but the authors find no academic references supporting that claim. SWOT is more usually traced to Selznick, Chandler, Andrews, Ansoff and Harvard business-policy teaching, with later contributions by Weihrich, Dealtry, and Wheelen and Hunger. It is also the main instrument of Mintzberg's design school. Selznick's 1957 book linked internal state to external expectations through distinctive competence, and Chandler's 1962 Strategy and Structure tied strategy to structure.

Continuation of the history. Chandler argued that environmental variables shape strategy. From the mid-1960s Harvard's business-policy course matched strengths and weaknesses to opportunities and threats, and Kenneth Andrews made the elements known under the SWOT acronym; his group's 1965 textbook Business Policy: Text and Cases became the design school's dominant text. Ansoff's 1965 Corporate Strategy broke SWOT into steps and introduced the product-market (Ansoff) matrix. In the 1980s SWOT spread to small business and marketing plans, and Weihrich (1982) introduced the TOWS matrix. In the 1990s it reached regional development and NGOs; Dealtry (1992) proposed Dynamic SWOT Analysis, and Wheelen and Hunger (1998) the SFAS matrix combining EFAS and IFAS tables. After the 1990s, criticism of strategic planning led to variants (WOTSUP, SOFT) and to combining SWOT with many other techniques, from the Balanced Scorecard, QFD and Porter's models to AHP, ANP and fuzzy and multi-criteria methods; the list runs on into the next block.

End of the list of complementary techniques (including MADM, PEAK with SETS, radar screens, TRIZ, Delphi panels and contrast mining) and of alternatives to SWOT (VRIO, Goals Grid, Telescopic Observations, SCORE and SORF), then Section 5 on SWOT's advantages. The authors list these: it gives a general perspective, a road map from general to specific; it allows macro evaluation of positive and negative internal and external factors together, as a two-by-two matrix (Table 6, from Chermack and Kasshanna, not in the text layer); it helps uncover opportunities and manage threats; it gives managers a thinking model and a basis for decisions; it fits other tools such as Porter's five forces, Delphi panels and the Balanced Scorecard; it encourages group discussion; it moves discussion beyond daily problems; and it can be applied at individual, organisational, national and international levels.

Section 6, disadvantages and limitations. Critics say SWOT only describes the current situation, and Hill and Westbrook called it expired. The disadvantages listed, from several sources: Weihrich argued it should be TOWS, starting from external factors; listing strengths on paper is prone to bias; it is general and was developed for stable conditions, so change undermines its entries; it is often poorly formulated and needs training, with Mintzberg's image of executives discussing strengths like students in a case class; it yields many factors without priorities, which multi-criteria methods (AHP, ANP, fuzzy variants, SMART, SMAA-O, MADM and others) try to remedy by ranking and weighting; it costs much time for little benefit; factors are hard to assign to one quadrant, as a strength can also be a weakness or an untaken opportunity become a threat; and it starts from current factors rather than those expected for the planning period.

Remaining disadvantages, the limitations and the start of the conclusion. SWOT lacks a quantitative benchmark against competitors, and its content can be distorted by corporate culture and the hopes of those involved. Following Dess and colleagues, Koch and King, the limitations are that strengths may not lead to advantage, the view of the environment can be too narrow, it is a static snapshot of a moving target, it can overemphasise a single dimension of strategy, and it is rarely applied below the organisation level. The authors judge SWOT useful but only as a starting point for fuller analysis. The conclusion restates that SWOT has been used for some fifty years to identify internal and external factors favourable or unfavourable to an objective, that internal analysis finds resources to develop and external analysis aligns strategy with the environment, and that properly used it gives a good basis for strategy formulation.

End of the conclusion and the reference list. The authors note that SWOT gives only a list of qualitative factors that is hard to use in decisions, that the literature finds SWOT alone insufficient and recommends combining qualitative and quantitative methods, and that little work has examined its history, advantages and limitations, which this article aims to cover. The references are 36 author entries (among them Andrews, Chandler, David, Dealtry, Hill and Westbrook, Humphrey, Mintzberg, Selznick, Thompson and Strickland, Weihrich's TOWS paper, and Wheelen and Hunger) and three unsigned web sources: the Merriam-Webster entry for "acronym" and two Nike SWOT pages.
